direct:shortest clean: From "P and Q" conclude P: one forward step (∧-elimination).
direct:typical: Apply the second premise to the first (modus ponens); a typical K12 direct proof is this short.
and_intro:shortest clean: To prove "P and (P or Q)", prove each conjunct: P is given, and "P or Q" follows from P.
and_intro:typical: Each conjunct gets its own short forward derivation (modus ponens, then ∨-introduction for the first).
cond_proof:shortest clean: To prove "if S then S or Q", assume S and derive "S or Q".
cond_proof:typical: Typical of K12: two assumptions are opened and never used; the consequent follows from the premises alone.
or_intro:shortest clean: "S or not S" follows from the given "not S" by ∨-introduction: excluded middle's shape without its classical content.
or_intro:typical: Weaken the premise to a longer disjunction in one step.
cases:shortest clean: In the case "P and S" extract S; in the case S there is nothing to do; either way S.
cases:typical: Typical of K12: the premises are inconsistent, the split is on a disjunction obtained by explosion, and one case ignores its assumption, so the split does no work.
disj_syll:shortest clean: Of the cases ¬S and P, the first contradicts the premise ¬¬S, so the goal follows from P.
disj_syll:typical: The proof first builds "Q or P" from P and then rules out the case Q against ¬Q: a disjunctive syllogism the proof did not need.
neg_intro:shortest clean: Assume ¬R; then "R or ¬R" holds, contradicting the premise; so ¬¬R, a proof of a negation with no classical step.
neg_intro:typical: Typical of K12: the premises are already inconsistent, so the negation is proved without using its assumption.
mod_tollens:shortest clean: From "if R then S" and "not S" conclude "not R": assuming R would give S.
mod_tollens:typical: Modus tollens with a compound antecedent: assuming ¬¬(S → R) yields a conjunction that the second premise denies.
ex_falso:shortest clean: Q and not Q are both given, so anything follows, here R.
ex_falso:typical: The premises Q and ¬(Q ∧ Q) contradict each other, so the goal follows by explosion.
contradiction:shortest clean: To prove R, assume ¬R and split on the first premise: R contradicts ¬R, and "¬R or ¬S" contradicts the second premise; so R. One of the 59 working reductios in K12.
contradiction:typical: Typical of K12: the premise already says "¬G implies falsum", and assuming ¬G only to apply it is double-negation elimination in disguise (a template).
contradiction:kind vacuous: The premises contradict each other; the reductio's assumption is never used (explosion in disguise).
contradiction:kind pointless: S is a premise, yet the proof re-derives S by assuming ¬S and contradicting the premise.
contradiction:kind scaffolded: The premise is ¬¬X; assuming ¬X only to clash with it is double-negation elimination in disguise.
contradiction:kind neg_goal: The goal is a negation, ¬S, reached through ¬¬¬S; intuitionistic logic already gives ¬S from that.
contradiction:kind free: A working reductio of a positive goal with no double negation supplied: the kind σ-covered theorems require.
dne:shortest clean: The premise ¬¬(Q ∨ R) gives Q ∨ R by double-negation elimination.
dne:typical: Eliminates a double negation that the theorem supplies (through its second premise), reached by an unnecessary case split.
lem:shortest clean: Excluded middle for X = ¬¬P, proved the standard way: assume it fails, refute ¬¬P, then refute the assumption (from the RL pools' textbook schemata; K12 has no clean instance).
lemma_reuse:shortest clean: The lemma ¬¬(Q → P) is proved once and used twice, once in each conjunct.
lemma_reuse:typical: The disjunction (P → P) ∨ S is derived once and reused three times.
